Re: Paula Wisniewski, DOB 03/09/1979. Seen 02/24/2025.

Voice remains normal. Anxiety steady and manageable with CBT skills; GAD-7 7. Her main complaint is sleep: despite consistent sleep hygiene and CBT strategies she takes one to two hours to fall asleep most nights and wakes repeatedly, and she is struggling to function at school. Restless legs contribute on some nights.

After discussing risks, including dependence, rebound insomnia and the need never to stop abruptly, we are starting alprazolam 2 mg at bedtime for insomnia. She will continue weekly therapy. Advised no alcohol with it and no driving if drowsy.

Current medications: carbidopa-levodopa 25/100 TID, ferrous sulfate 325 mg daily, loratadine as needed, levonorgestrel IUD, and now alprazolam 2 mg at bedtime.
Follow-up in 3 months.
Outpatient psychiatry

documents.title: Office Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
45F (46 next week). Two months of getting steadily more tired, lightheaded when she stands quickly, and she can't keep up on her usual walk with her husband; stairs at school are hard again. No recent illness, no fever, no weight loss, no diarrhea, no abdominal pain, no black or bloody stools. Periods light since the IUD, not heavy at all. Nosebleeds the usual once a week or so, short.

Notable: last summer (late July into August) she spent about four weeks in a rural farming village in northeastern Brazil with a volunteer agriculture program. Worked barefoot in the fields a lot, no clean water or real sanitation where they stayed. No travel since.

New since last visit: psychiatry started alprazolam 2 mg qhs last week for sleep.
Meds: carbidopa-levodopa 25-100 TID; ferrous sulfate 325 daily; loratadine prn; LNG-IUD; alprazolam 2 mg qhs.

Exam: pale. Orthostatics not done; seated HR as recorded. Not in distress, hemodynamically stable. No scleral icterus. No cervical, axillary or inguinal lymphadenopathy. Heart RRR. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft, nontender, no hepatosplenomegaly. Skin no rash.

CBC back before she left the building: Hgb 7.2, Hct 23, MCV 68.

A/P:
1. Severe microcytic anemia, a big drop from 12.6 in September despite light periods. With barefoot work in rural Brazil, hookworm is high on the list. Stool O&P sent today. Iron studies, CMP pending. IV iron ordered.
2. Hemodynamically ok, no chest pain or syncope, so no transfusion today. ED precautions reviewed: chest pain, fainting, shortness of breath at rest.
3. Insomnia: on alprazolam per psychiatry, noted.
Call when stool back.

documents.title: Question
documents.author: patient
documents.body: If it turns out to be a parasite, can my husband catch it from me? Should I stay home from school? I feel ok to work, just tired.

documents.title: RE: Question
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Good questions. If it is hookworm, it isn't passed from person to person at home or at school, because the eggs need weeks in warm soil before they can infect anyone. You don't need to stay home. Regular handwashing is always good. We'll call as soon as the stool test is back.

documents.title: Emergency Department Physician Record
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
Patient: Paula Wisniewski, 46F. Arrived 10:20 by private car with husband.

CC: anxiety, shaking, racing heart.

HPI: 46-year-old woman with hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia, Parkinson disease, functional neurological disorder and generalized anxiety disorder, last seen by her PCP in March 2025 for a hookworm infection. Over the past 24 hours, steadily worsening anxiety, tremor and palpitations. She has been taking alprazolam 2 mg at bedtime for insomnia for about six months. Her prescription ran out and she has taken none for the last 3 nights. No seizure, no hallucinations, no chest pain, no syncope. No alcohol in the past week. No other new medications.

PMH: HHT, Parkinson disease, functional neurological disorder (voice, resolved), generalized anxiety disorder, iron deficiency anemia, allergic rhinitis, restless legs.
Meds: carbidopa-levodopa 25-100 TID, alprazolam 2 mg qhs (not taken x3 days), ferrous sulfate 325 daily, loratadine prn, LNG-IUD.
Allergies: no known drug allergies; shellfish.
Social: never smoker; 1-2 glasses of wine a week; teaches high school mathematics.

Triage vitals: BP 160/95, HR 110, RR 22, T 37.8 C (100 F), SpO2 98% RA.
Exam: agitated, diaphoretic, visibly tremulous. Pupils equal, reactive. Mucous membranes moist. Heart tachycardic, regular, no murmur. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft, nontender. Neuro: alert and oriented x3, no focal weakness; increased tone in all extremities with brisk, hyperreflexic reflexes; no clonus. Speech normal.

Data: Na 140, K 4.2, Cl 102, HCO3 24, BUN 18, Cr 0.9, glucose 98, Ca 9.2, Mg 2.0. CBC within normal limits. ECG sinus tachycardia, otherwise normal.

Course: lorazepam 2 mg IV at 10:50 with clear improvement in tremor and agitation over the next hour. Observed for several hours; by discharge HR 84, BP 128/80, afebrile, calm, tremor resolved.

Impression: benzodiazepine withdrawal after abrupt cessation of alprazolam.
Disposition: discharged home with husband. Resume alprazolam 2 mg at bedtime tonight (short supply provided until psychiatry renews); do not stop abruptly; any taper only under the prescriber's direction. Return for seizure, confusion, hallucinations or worsening symptoms. Follow up with PCP this week and contact psychiatry on the next business day.

Emergency medicine

documents.title: Emergency Department Physician Record
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
Patient: Paula Wisniewski, 46F.

CC: nosebleed that won't stop.

HPI: 46-year-old woman with hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia and iron deficiency anemia, seen by her PCP last week for near-daily nosebleeds with hemoglobin 8.3. Woke at 5 am bleeding from the right nostril, still going after more than 45 minutes of pressure. Lightheaded. No chest pain. Not on antiplatelets or anticoagulants.
PMH: HHT, iron deficiency anemia, Parkinson disease, generalized anxiety disorder, functional neurological disorder, restless legs, allergic rhinitis (loratadine as needed).
Meds (per pharmacy list): carbidopa-levodopa 25-100 TID, alprazolam 2 mg qhs, ferrous sulfate 325 daily.
Allergies: no known drug allergies.

Triage: BP 118/74, HR 98, SpO2 99%. Pale, oozing from right anterior naris.
Nasal: bleeding from right anterior septum. Controlled with oxymetazoline-soaked pledgets and 20 minutes of continuous pressure; no packing placed given HHT. No posterior bleeding.

Labs: Hgb 6.8, Hct 22. PT/INR normal. Type and crossmatch.

Course:
09:20 Hemostasis holding. Symptomatic anemia: 2 units PRBC ordered, consent obtained.
11:20 Unit 1 started.
11:35 About 15 minutes into the transfusion she reported itching, and raised erythematous wheals appeared on the trunk and both arms. She denied difficulty breathing, voice change or throat closing. BP 125/80, HR 88, RR 16, afebrile. No wheeze, no stridor, no lip or tongue swelling. Transfusion stopped immediately; line kept open with saline. Diphenhydramine 50 mg IV. Blood bank notified, transfusion reaction workup sent.
12:10 Hives fading, itch resolved.
Transfusion reaction workup: clerical and ABO/Rh recheck concordant; direct antiglobulin test negative; post-reaction plasma without visible hemolysis; urinalysis negative for blood. No evidence of an acute hemolytic reaction. Blood bank: mild allergic (urticarial) reaction.
16:30 After diphenhydramine 25 mg IV premedication, a new unit started slowly; completed 19:15 without any reaction.
21:10 Post-transfusion Hgb 7.7. No recurrent bleeding.

Impression:
1. Epistaxis from HHT, controlled.
2. Symptomatic iron deficiency anemia, transfused 1 unit PRBC.
3. Allergic (urticarial) transfusion reaction; acute hemolytic transfusion reaction excluded.

Disposition: home 21:50 with husband. Blood bank note added: premedicate with an antihistamine for future transfusions. PCP follow-up within 2-3 days; ENT and hematology referrals already placed by PCP, keep those. Return for bleeding not controlled with 20 minutes of pressure, fainting, chest pain, rash or breathing trouble.

Emergency medicine

documents.title: Hematology Consultation
documents.author: hematology
documents.body:
Re: Paula Wisniewski, DOB 03/09/1979. Seen 11/12/2025.

46-year-old woman with HHT, recurrent iron deficiency anemia, a hookworm infection treated this spring, and an ED visit on 11/3 for epistaxis requiring transfusion (hemoglobin 6.8, urticarial reaction to the first unit, hemolysis excluded). Two prior courses of IV iron, 2024 and 2025, each with a good response. Menses now minimal on a levonorgestrel IUD; GI evaluation in 2024 with normal EGD and colonoscopy.

Assessment: iron deficiency anemia driven by HHT epistaxis, now the dominant source of loss.

Plan:
1. Ferric carboxymaltose 750 mg IV on 11/13 and 11/20 at our infusion center.
2. CBC and ferritin every 3 months, drawn at her PCP's lab; goal to keep ferritin above 50 with repeat IV iron as needed.
3. Continue oral iron if tolerated.
4. ENT for the nose is the key to reducing losses.
5. Any future transfusion: premedicate with an antihistamine.
Follow-up with labs in February.

Hematology

documents.title: Otolaryngology Consultation
documents.author: ENT
documents.body:
Re: Paula Wisniewski, DOB 03/09/1979. Seen 12/09/2025.

HHT with nosebleeds since adolescence, cauterized once at 25, near-daily since October with an ED visit and transfusion on 11/3. Now 2-3 short bleeds a week after IV iron and humidification.

Exam: anterior rhinoscopy and nasal endoscopy show multiple small telangiectasias over the anterior septum on both sides, more on the right, with a fresh crust on the right. No septal perforation. Posterior nasal cavity and nasopharynx unremarkable. Oral cavity with a few small telangiectasias on the lip and tongue tip.

Assessment: HHT-related epistaxis from anterior septal telangiectasias.
Plan: continue nightly saline gel and bedroom humidification; avoid nose blowing hard and nasal steroid sprays. In-office laser coagulation of the anterior septal telangiectasias under topical anesthesia, scheduled 1/13/2026. Avoid chemical or electrocautery and non-absorbable packing.

Otolaryngology
